text.p: Canadians began voting on Monday, in a general election that pollsters say could give budget-slashing Prime Minister Jean Chretien a new but reduced mandate.

The sun shone across much of the country as the population chose a new House of Commons. Chretien's Liberals maintained a substantial lead over the other four main parties in polls before the weekend but analysts said they could suffer a reduced majority or possibly even a minority of the 301 seats.

Chretien had called the election 1-1/2 years before constitutionally necessary because of his strong lead in the polls, but a combination of attacks from his four main rivals and what analysts call a campaign without an imperative has cut into his margin.

He swept the Conservatives out of power in 1993 with 177 of 295 seats. But polls indicated a failure to expand his weak base in the West and suggested the Conservatives could crack his grip on the maritime provinces in the East.

His opponents attacked his government's handling of unemployment which during his entire mandate was stuck above the nine percent rate. On the right, the Conservatives and Reform called for tax cuts while on the left the New Democrats suggested stimulative spending.
Polls suggested the western-based Reform Party would win the second highest number of seats, enabling it to replace the secessionist Bloc Quebecois as the official opposition in Parliament.
